metadata.title: International Comparative Study on PISA Mathematics Achievement Test Based on Cognitive Diagnostic Models

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 mathematics assessment data for a cross-national comparison across 10 participating countries, selecting a subset of students who completed 12 specific mathematics items. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or any replicate-weight scheme, so it is unclear whether population-representative estimates were produced. Because the analysis is based on cognitive diagnostic model estimation (CDM) using item responses and a constructed Q-matrix, the paper does not describe any weighting variable (such as W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or how weights would be incorporated into the estimation. Analysts using PISA microdata should apply the standard PISA student weights when producing population-representative country estimates, but this paper’s weighting strategy is not documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent quantities are cognitive attribute mastery probabilities/states estimated via cognitive diagnostic models (CDMs) rather than PV-based achievement scores from PISA’s IRT scaling. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure for item-response data (e.g., exclusion rules for incomplete item sets), which is a reporting gap given that CDM estimation typically requires complete response patterns for the selected items.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study selected 12 mathematics items from PISA 2012 that were publicly available and jointly tested across the 10 countries. Only students who completed these 12 items all at the same time were included. Countries that participated in PISA 2012 mathematics but did not take these 12 items (e.g., Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Argentina, and other South American countries) were excluded from the comparative analysis, and no data from Antarctica were available. The manuscript does not specify additional exclusions (e.g., missing responses within the 12 items) beyond the requirement that students completed the 12 items.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Mathematics (15-year-olds) — 12 selected items across 10 countries
main_findings.target_variable: Cognitive diagnostic model fit (best model selection)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison (Table 3): LLM has smallest Deviation (28229.28), AIC (32419.22), and BIC (44579.13) among evaluated models (DINA, DINO, RRUM, ACDM, LCDM, G-DINA, Mixed Model).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics data (12 selected items across 10 countries), the study compared multiple cognitive diagnostic models to evaluate model fit and found that the LLM had the smallest Deviation, AIC, and BIC. This indicates that adopting the LLM framework can provide more accurate fine-grained attribute mastery diagnostics for PISA mathematics item sets, supporting curriculum and remediation decisions based on attribute-level strengths and weaknesses.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Proportional mastery (Table 4): China highest for N1 (0.740), N2 (0.743), N3 (0.749); Japan highest for N4 (0.886) with China second (0.882).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study estimated mastery probabilities for four content attributes (N1–N4) and found that China led in N1–N3 while Japan led in N4 (data and uncertainty), with China close behind. This indicates that country-specific mathematics content priorities may be warranted—e.g., strengthening data/uncertainty instruction in China while leveraging China’s relative strengths in change/relationships, space/shape, and quantity for other contexts.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Proportional mastery (Table 4): P3 highest in Japan (0.636) and China (0.771 for P3? as shown: China P3=0.771; Japan P3=0.636; Singapore P3=0.661; United States P3=0.522; Saudi Arabia P3=0.248). Narrative summary: P3 generally better than P1 and P2; US and Saudi Arabia lowest in process attributes.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study estimated mastery probabilities for three process attributes (P1 mathematization, P2 mathematical operation, P3 realization) and found that P3 mastery was generally higher than P1 and P2, with China and Japan/Singapore showing stronger process mastery while the United States and Saudi Arabia were lower. This indicates that instructional interventions may benefit from emphasizing the specific process components where mastery is weakest (especially mathematization for lower-performing countries), rather than treating process skills as a single undifferentiated construct.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Proportional mastery (Table 4): China highest for C1 (0.693), C2 (0.796), and C4 (0.737); Japan highest for C3 (0.897). Saudi Arabia lowest across contexts (C1=0.223, C2=0.381, C3=0.238, C4=0.238).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study estimated mastery probabilities for four context attributes (personal, occupational, societal, scientific) and found that China led in personal/occupational/scientific contexts while Japan led in societal contexts, with Saudi Arabia showing comparatively low mastery across all contexts. This indicates that context-sensitive mathematics teaching—especially occupational and societal applications—may be a key lever for improving mathematics performance equity across countries.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Narrative results: linear prerequisite patterns supported for content (N4 → N3 → N2 → N1) in most countries; process attributes show P3 as prerequisite (P3 → P2 → P1) in almost all data; context attributes show societal (C3) as prerequisite in all countries except Singapore. Example trajectory (Figure 4/description): for China main trajectory (0000) → (0001) → (0011) → (1011) → (1111).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics the study derived hierarchical learning trajectories from estimated knowledge states and found consistent prerequisite ordering for content (N4→N3→N2→N1) and process (P3→P2→P1), with societal context (C3) acting as a prerequisite in most countries. This indicates that remediation and curriculum sequencing can be designed around attribute prerequisites (starting with uncertainty/data and building toward change/relationships), though the cross-sectional nature limits causal claims about learning over time.

data.outcome_summary: This study conducts an international cognitive diagnostic analysis of PISA 2012 mathematics using 12 publicly available items that were jointly tested across 10 countries (GBR, FIN, RUS, CHN, JPN, SGP, USA, CAN, AUS, and Saudi Arabia). Students were included if they completed all 12 items, yielding 24,512 students total. The authors evaluated eight cognitive diagnostic model families (DINA, DINO, RRUM, ACDM, LCDM, LLM, G-DINA, and a Mixtures Model) and selected the LLM because it had the smallest Deviation, AIC, and BIC. Using LLM with Bayesian EAP estimation, they reported attribute mastery probabilities for content (N1–N4), process (P1–P3), and context (C1–C4), plus knowledge-state patterns and prerequisite learning trajectories (e.g., N4→N3→N2→N1; P3→P2→P1). The paper does not document survey-weight use or missing-data handling, and the learning trajectories are derived from cross-sectional data, so associations cannot be interpreted causally.
